items.t: AIA stock: Group launches cancer cover as HSBC keeps Hold
sum: AIA Group's Hong Kong and Macau business launched a new cancer-drug insurance plan on November 9, while HSBC retained a cautious view of the insurer. The developments give investors two distinct signals: product expansion in health protection and a restrained external assessment of the shares.

In a press release, AIA Hong Kong & Macau said FutureShield reimburses eligible cancer drugs and supportive medications prescribed for active or palliative treatment. Coverage applies in public hospitals in Hong Kong and Macau and in hospitals in mainland China.

The plan offers a lifetime cancer limit of up to HK$5 million and simplified underwriting without a medical examination. AIA also highlighted cross-border support for identifying providers and coordinating appointments. The product strengthens the group's healthcare proposition, although its commercial contribution will depend on customer uptake, claims experience and pricing.

Markets Insider reported that HSBC maintained its Hold rating on AIA Group in a report released on November 9 and set a price target of HK$83. The report cited an analyst consensus of Strong Buy with a consensus target of HK$100.62.

The gap between HSBC's stance and the broader consensus underlines differing expectations about AIA's earnings momentum and valuation. Investors will likely focus on new-business trends, regional sales and the effect of product initiatives on future profitability.

HSBC downgrades Nvidia, says stock to struggle until new CEO named
sum: Nvidia is going to struggle until it gets a new CEO to permanently replace Jensen Huang and take over from CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress, according to HSBC. Analyst Frank Lee downgraded the chipmaker to hold from buy. His price target of $170, down from $365, implies upside of just 2.3% from Thursday's close. "We believe the uncertainties will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out and the new CEO is able to demonstrate execution capabilities," Lee said in a Friday note to clients. Lee thinks tightened export restrictions on the company's products are serious possibility, which could dent Nvidia's fiscal year 2028 earnings per share by 13%. NVDA 5D mountain NVDA 5-day chart "During the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the US and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions," he said. "Our sensitivity implies that if NVIDIA loses 11% of FY28e revenue, its EPS downside could be 13% compared with our base case EPS of USD15.65. The bear case EPS of USD13.57 is 14% below current consensus of USD15.77." Huang left the company amid suspicions that he had had an affair with a Chinese spy, though the Chinese government has dismissed such claims. The New York Times also reported that Huang had a relationship with a person who reported to him. Reuters later reported that Huang had an " intimate relationship " with a second employee. Nvidia, which makes top-of-the-line graphics processing units, is perhaps the linchpin of the global AI supply chain. It has been called the " central bank of AI ," maintaining investments in its own customers alongside financing platforms with some of the biggest names in private credit . Shares fell more than 4% following HSBC's downgrade. HSBC joined a slew of banks and Wall Street research firms that lowered their rating on the stock this week. Among them are Truist , Evercore ISI, William Blair, Oppenheimer and Bernstein .

items.t: HSBC stock outlook holds after strong third-quarter profit growth
sum: HSBC's third-quarter results show broad-based growth across its businesses, while management kept the bank's medium-term targets unchanged. The update was published for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, with the latest investor information available on Friday, November 13.
HSBC stock traded at 16.23 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:43 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026, 0.06 percent above the Xetra close of Thursday, November 12, at 16.22 euros.

According to HSBC's investor update, revenue excluding notable items rose 5 percent to 18.7 billion US dollars in the third quarter. Profit before tax excluding notable items increased 10 percent to 10.0 billion US dollars, while annualised return on tangible equity reached 18.8 percent year to date.

The performance extended across the group's main businesses. Fee and other income in wholesale transaction banking increased 11 percent year on year. Net new money in Asia's wealth business reached 38 billion US dollars during the quarter, taking year-to-date flows above 100 billion US dollars.

HSBC also reported deposit growth of 105 billion US dollars during the quarter, including held-for-sale balances. Deposits in Hong Kong rose by 21 billion US dollars, while commercial lending in the United Kingdom increased 13 percent year on year.

Management reiterated its target of revenue growth rising to 5 percent year on year by 2028, excluding notable items and on a constant-currency basis. The bank continues to target annualised return on tangible equity of at least 17 percent and a dividend payout ratio of 50 percent, also excluding relevant notable items.

The board approved a third interim dividend for 2026 of 10 US cents per share. HSBC also intends to initiate a further share buyback of up to 1 billion US dollars, which it expects to complete by the announcement of its 2026 full-year results.

IIFL Finance Share Price: NBFC stock jumps after Rs 6,414 crore Blackstone deal; MOFSL, HSBC see up to 33% upside
sum: IIFL Finance shares rose over 2 per cent in early trade on Wednesday after the company announced a Rs 6,414 crore primary equity investment led by Blackstone, one of the largest private equity infusions in a listed Indian non-banking financial company (NBFC).
The stock was trading at Rs 640.50, up Rs 13.50, or 2.15 per cent, on the NSE on November 11.

The proposed investment includes Rs 5,000 crore from Blackstone, Rs 1,264 crore from the company's promoters and Rs 150 crore from Anchorage Capital. The transaction is expected to strengthen IIFL Finance's capital position and support the expansion of its secured lending businesses.
IIFL Finance's board approved a primary capital raise of Rs 6,414 crore through a preferential issue at its meeting on November 10.

Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore through compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) for an approximately 16 per cent stake in the company on a fully diluted basis. The preference shares will convert into equity shares at Rs 602 apiece within 18 months of allotment.

The company's promoters, Nirmal Jain and R Venkataraman, will invest Rs 1,264 crore through a preferential allotment of warrants. Anchorage Capital will participate in the transaction with a primary equity investment of Rs 150 crore.
The company said the entire investment would be infused as primary capital. The proposed transaction is subject to customary regulatory and shareholder approvals.

HSBC stock: Capital relief strengthens buyback outlook
sum: HSBC is pairing unchanged full-year guidance with additional capital flexibility after a broad-based third quarter. In its investor and analyst call published on October 30, HSBC said it was on track to meet its targets and had approved a further share buyback of up to 1 billion US dollars.

Group Chief Financial Officer Pam Kaur said the bank expects Basel 3.1 to provide an estimated benefit to its common equity tier 1 ratio from January 1, 2027. HSBC said the capital relief, together with fourth-quarter capital generation, should leave it well positioned for growth and shareholder distributions.

The bank continues to target a 14 percent to 14.5 percent operating range for its CET1 ratio. Management also reiterated a 50 percent dividend payout ratio and described buybacks as its preferred residual method of returning capital.

HSBC said it delivered 0.2 billion US dollars of simplification savings during the quarter, bringing cumulative savings to 1.9 billion US dollars against its 2 billion US dollar target. The bank remains on track for target-basis cost growth of 1 percent in 2026.

Revenue excluding notable items increased 5 percent to 18.7 billion US dollars in the third quarter, while profit before tax on the same basis rose 10 percent to 10 billion US dollars. HSBC said all four businesses grew deposits and each generated annualized return on tangible equity above 17 percent, excluding notable items.

Deposits increased by 105 billion US dollars over the preceding 12 months, including held-for-sale balances. In Asia, wealth net new money reached 38 billion US dollars in the quarter and more than 95 billion US dollars year to date. The bank maintained its full-year credit guidance of around 45 basis points and its banking net interest income guidance of at least 46 billion US dollars.

The figures and management commentary are available in the HSBC investor and analyst call. The unchanged targets reduce the scope for a near-term guidance upgrade, while the planned buyback and potential capital relief support the bank's capital-return profile.

When someone applies for a credit card, loan or car finance, a lender must decide quickly whether they’re likely to repay. That’s where it shines.

sum: HSBC Holdings (LSE:HSBA) has been active in its funding stack, redeeming higher coupon US$2.25b senior notes while issuing new fixed to floating securities. For shareholders, the key question is how this reshapes interest costs and capital flexibility.

These funding moves come after a run of frequent announcements from HSBC Holdings, from Q3 2026 earnings and dividend confirmations in late October to multiple fixed income offerings across the US dollar market. The share price has eased about 7.3% over the past month and around 14.7% over 90 days, while the year-to-date share price return of 9.5% and a 1-year total shareholder return of 27.2% reflect momentum over a longer horizon, with total shareholder return over 3 and 5 years described as extremely strong in absolute terms.

Scan how HSBC Holdings compares on balance sheet strength and funding resilience with a curated list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (9 results) tailored for investors watching capital structure moves like these.

HSBC Holdings has reshaped its funding mix while the share price has pulled back, leaving a clear gap between the market level and published fair value estimates. Where does a reasonable fair value range actually land now?
On the narrative view, HSBC Holdings screens as undervalued, with a fair value of £15.15 against a last close of £13.05, which leaves a sizeable gap for investors to judge.

Strong capital generation, a CET1 ratio around the 14% target range, a 40 to 50 basis point CET1 uplift expected from Basel 3.1 and resumed share buybacks together point to scope for continued capital returns alongside reinvestment. This can support per share earnings and distributions.
Still, deposit competition in Hong Kong and the UK and the planned US$2.2b revenue removal from 15 exits could both challenge the HSBC Holdings undervaluation story.

sum: Shares of Bharti Airtel Ltd rose over 2 per cent on Friday, November 6, after the telecom major reported a 31 per cent year-on-year (YoY) increase in consolidated net profit for the September quarter (Q2FY27).

The stock was trading at Rs 2,101.40 on the NSE, up Rs 44.50 or 2.16 per cent. It opened at Rs 2,120 and touched an intraday high of Rs 2,120 and a low of Rs 2,076.20. The company's market capitalisation stood at around Rs 12.58 lakh crore.
Bharti Airtel announced its Q2 results after market hours on Thursday.
The company's consolidated net profit rose to Rs 8,887.5 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 6,791.6 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
Revenue from operations increased 16.7 per cent YoY to Rs 60,878 crore from Rs 52,145 crore in Q2FY26.

Operating performance also remained strong. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) grew 17.8 per cent YoY to Rs 35,240 crore from Rs 29,919 crore in the year-ago quarter.

India revenue increased 9.4 per cent YoY to Rs 42,308 crore. The mobile business continued to benefit from premiumisation, higher average revenue per user (ARPU) and additions in smartphone data customers.

sum: HSBC said it had revised its expectations for margin expansion in India and now sees international operations as a larger growth opportunity than it had previously anticipated. The brokerage has retained its valuation multiple for India while assigning a higher multiple to the international business.

Shares of Lenskart Solutions Ltd. opened with gains of over 6% on Thursday, November 5, after several brokerages maintained or upgraded their positive stance on the company following its strong September quarter (Q2 FY27) performance.

Nomura has maintained a 'Buy' rating on Lenskart with a price target of ₹888, while HSBC has upgraded the stock to 'Buy' and raised its price target to ₹790. CLSA has an 'Outperform' rating with a target of ₹773, while Jefferies has maintained its 'Buy' rating with a price target of ₹780.

Nomura said Lenskart's Q2 FY27 performance was ahead of estimates, with consolidated sales growing 32.5% year-on-year. EBITDA, before accounting for Ind AS 116, increased 65% year-on-year, while the corresponding margin expanded 270 basis points to 13.8%, supported by operating leverage across both India and international operations.

In India, strong same-store sales growth, in-house manufacturing and rental leverage supported margin improvement. International operations also delivered volume-led growth, with pre-Ind AS EBITDA margins remaining in double digits.
The brokerage highlighted several initiatives aimed at driving long-term volume growth of 20% and achieving an operating margin of 25%.

HSBC upgraded Lenskart to 'Buy' and raised its price target to ₹790. The brokerage said that EBITDA was 3% ahead of consensus estimates, with India same-store sales growth at 21% and international operations sustaining growth of 23% in constant currency terms.

items.t: HSBC stock: Q3 profit jumps as buyback and outlook hold
sum: HSBC Holdings reported stronger third-quarter results on October 27, 2026, while keeping its financial targets unchanged. In its 3Q26 earnings release, the bank said profit before tax increased 32 percent from a year earlier to 9.6 billion US dollars.

The headline increase included a favorable 1.4 billion US dollar effect from notable items, mainly because legal provisions recorded in the third quarter of 2025 did not recur. Excluding notable items, constant-currency profit before tax rose by 0.9 billion US dollars to 10.0 billion US dollars. Profit after tax increased 38 percent to 7.6 billion US dollars.

Revenue rose 0.8 billion US dollars to 18.6 billion US dollars, driven mainly by banking net interest income. HSBC also cited higher fee and other income in Corporate and Institutional Banking, Wealth and other businesses. Revenue excluding notable items on a constant-currency basis increased to 18.7 billion US dollars.

Net interest income advanced 6 percent to 9.3 billion US dollars, while banking net interest income increased by 0.6 billion US dollars to 11.7 billion US dollars. The net interest margin held steady at 1.57 percent. Expected credit losses fell 17 percent to 0.8 billion US dollars, although the bank continued to monitor commercial real estate and other credit exposures.

HSBC stock traded at 15.75 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:47 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 4.30 percent above the Xetra close of Tuesday, November 3, at 15.10 euros. Investors can follow the real-time quote of HSBC stock.

The board approved a third interim dividend of 0.10 US dollars per share. HSBC completed a 1 billion US dollar buyback on September 28 and intends to start another repurchase of up to 1 billion US dollars, which it expects to complete by the announcement of its 2026 full-year results.

Management retained its target for banking net interest income of at least 46 billion US dollars in 2026. It also maintained a return on average tangible equity target of 17 percent or better for 2026 through 2028, excluding notable items, and a 50 percent dividend payout ratio target through 2028.

HSBC shares slide almost 7% as revenue misses and wealth stalls despite 32% profit jump
sum: - HSBC reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, October 27, and the shares fell almost 7% even though profit rose sharply.

- HSBC shares fell almost 7% after Q3 revenue of around $18.6bn missed forecasts and wealth revenue stalled, overshadowing a 32% jump in pre-tax profit to around $9.6bn and a fresh buyback of up to $1bn. Guidance was only reaffirmed, not upgraded.

The sell-off shows how much was already priced into HSBC after a strong run. Without a guidance upgrade, a revenue miss and stalled wealth growth were enough to trigger profit-taking. The read-across for Hong Kong and Asian banks is margin pressure: costlier time deposits threaten interest income just as the Fed’s hiking path keeps funding costs high. Oil matters indirectly, since inflation and rate uncertainty linked to the Iran war is weighing on bank valuations broadly, and HSBC is already setting aside provisions for the Middle East conflict. The Basel 3.1 capital boost from January 2027 gives HSBC room to expand buybacks, which could limit further downside once the disappointment fades.
HSBC delivered a big profit jump and another $1 billion buyback, but a revenue miss, flat wealth income and no upgrade to its targets were enough to send the shares sharply lower.
- HSBC shares fell almost 7% on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue of around $18.6 billion missed forecasts of roughly $19.1 billion, and adjusted EPS of $2.10 missed $2.22.
- Pre-tax profit rose 32% to around $9.6 billion, helped by the absence of last year’s legal provisions. Excluding notable items, it rose about 10% to around $10 billion.
- Wealth revenue was flat at around $2.7 billion after strong growth in the first half. Net interest income rose 6% but was slightly below expectations.

Top Utilities Stocks to Watch: HSBC’s Preferred Picks
sum: Investing.com -- HSBC has identified five preferred utilities stocks positioned to benefit from surging electricity demand driven by data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. The investment bank rates all five companies as Buy, citing above-average growth prospects and strong execution capabilities in an evolving power landscape.

The utilities sector is experiencing a transformation as electricity demand accelerates, particularly in regions attracting large data center developments. HSBC's preferred stocks demonstrate rate base growth rates well above historical averages, with several companies projecting demand increases of 40% to 80% by 2030. The bank's selections span integrated electric utilities, transmission-focused operators, and diversified energy infrastructure companies across multiple U.S. markets.

1. Entergy (ETR) - HSBC rates Entergy as Buy with a target price of USD123.50, implying 17.5% upside. The integrated electric utility operates in Louisiana, Arkansas, Texas, Mississippi and New Orleans. HSBC forecasts 2026-30 rate base growth of 16% and earnings per share growth of 13%. The company's USD67 billion investment plan for 2026-30 includes plans to add approximately 30GW of new capacity through 2035. Louisiana drives growth with approximately 60% demand increase expected by 2030. HSBC considers execution risk low, citing the company's early supply chain management and standardized processes.

2. Pinnacle West (PNW) - HSBC rates Pinnacle West as Buy with a target price of USD119.50, implying 15.5% upside. The Arizona-based integrated utility is forecasted to achieve 2026-30 rate base growth of 12% and earnings per share growth of 13%. The company has recorded growth rates of 5% to 10% in the last six quarters and forecasts approximately 45% demand increase by 2030. HSBC notes execution risk as medium to high due to past regulatory challenges, but expects material improvements following a pivotal ratemaking decision before year-end 2026.

3. NextEra (NEE) - HSBC rates NextEra as Buy with a target price of USD103.00, implying 29.1% upside. The company targets capital expenditures of USD295-325 billion over 2025-32, with USD185-225 billion allocated to NextEra Energy Resources.

sum: HSBC Holdings (NYSE:HSBC), one of the world's largest banks with a dominant franchise across Asia, barely moved in Tuesday afternoon trading in Hong Kong despite posting another earnings beat. First-half pretax profit jumped 23% year over year to $19.5 billion, comfortably ahead of the $18.9 billion analysts had expected. The bank also restarted capital returns with a new share-buyback program worth up to $1 billion after sitting on the sidelines for the past three quarters. Investors, however, were clearly looking for more.
- Is HSBC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The first-half report had plenty of positives beneath the surface. HSBC raised its full-year net interest income guidance and now expects the figure to exceed $46 billion, up from its previous forecast of around that level. Wealth management continued firing on all cylinders, with revenue climbing 18% as affluent clients across Asia remained active. HSBC and Hang Seng Bank added roughly 640,000 new customers in Hong Kong during the period, while Corporate and Institutional Banking overtook every other division to contribute about one-third of the group's first-half profit. Management also revealed that more than 70 Asian IPOs are currently sitting in its deal pipeline, highlighting that capital-markets activity is beginning to recover across the region.

The attached GF Value chart adds another angle investors shouldn't ignore. While HSBC continues to deliver resilient earnings growth, GuruFocus estimates the stock's GF Value at $56.38 versus a recent market price of $106.32. That places the shares nearly 89% above their estimated intrinsic value and firmly in the "Significantly Overvalued" range. Strong businesses can stay expensive for long periods, but lofty valuations also leave less room for disappointment if growth slows.

That valuation backdrop helps explain why the stock failed to rally despite the earnings beat. HSBC shares retreated from their record high of HK$169.50 after investors focused on the size of the buyback instead. Citi analysts noted that the $1 billion repurchase authorization came in well below the roughly $2.2 billion the market had been expecting, overshadowing a pretax profit beat of around $600 million.

items.t: HSBC earnings beat estimates, company resumes stock buybacks
sum: HSBC Holdings reported first-half pretax profit of $19.5 billion on Tuesday, a 23% increase from a year earlier, as revenue growth in lending and wealth management drove earnings past analyst estimates.

Analysts had penciled in $18.9 billion, according to Reuters, making the result a beat. Profit after tax came in at $15.3 billion, up $2.9 billion from the first half of 2025. Revenue rose 11% to $37.7 billion.

Alongside the results, the bank announced it would restart share buybacks with a program capped at $1 billion, targeted for completion ahead of its third-quarter reporting date. The pause stretched across three quarters, tracing back to an October announcement that HSBC would acquire full ownership of Hang Seng Bank. That transaction closed in January at a price of nearly $14 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

"We delivered strong returns to our shareholders," Chief Executive Georges Elhedery said in a statement. "Our 18.2% annualised RoTE reflects a strong performance. We are paying another 10 cents per share quarterly interim dividend. We have also resumed share buy-backs (up to $1bn), three quarters after we paused them following the Hang Seng Bank privatisation announcement."
The board approved a second interim dividend of $0.10 per share, bringing the full first-half dividend to $0.20.

HSBC raised its banking net interest income guidance for 2026 to at least $46 billion, up from a prior forecast of around $46 billion, citing a continued favorable interest rate environment. Banking net interest income for the first half rose $1.6 billion to $22.9 billion, driven by deposit balance growth and the benefit of reinvestment of the bank's structural hedge at higher yields.

Wealth fee and other income grew 18% on a constant currency basis in the period. The corporate and institutional banking segment also posted growth, with wholesale transaction banking fee and other income rising 6% from a year earlier.

Heiress who sued Barclays, HSBC for alleged money laundering with Ghislaine Maxwell link seeks $15B in damages
sum: Barclays and HSBC have been accused of enabling a late real estate tycoon to siphon cash from trusts intended for his daughter into a massive money-laundering scheme — including deals that were brokered by an entity linked to Ghislaine Maxwell’s family, according to a bombshell court filing.

Tanya Dick-Stock and her husband Darrin Stock sued the banks in December, alleging they helped her late father John Dick Sr. turn trusts including one valued at $350 million into a piggy bank to facilitate illicit transactions for a rogue’s gallery that included two siblings of convicted child sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell.

In a new filing in Colorado federal court, the couple claims banks neglected their duty to “Know Your Customer,” or KYC, under the anti-fraud and money-laundering regulations that govern financial institutions They also claimed the fraud was larger than previously known, and sought another $3 billion on top of the original $12 billion they sought from the banks, factoring in interest and damages.

The “industry-wide money laundering schemes” could not have happened without “global banks willing to accept coded accounts, forgo meaningful and required … obligations, move funds without contemporaneous documentation, and process transactions whose true economic substance was deliberately obscured,” the new filing states.

Barclays and HSBC and some of their subsidiaries, plus a trust company called Zedra, allegedly tricked creditors, avoided taxes and hid cash through a since-shuttered offshore trust business called La Hougue, which later morphed into Pantrust.

The Stocks, who are repped by former presidential candidate and ex-Sen. John Edwards, previously claimed they found evidence of the fraud in a locked squash court on their former 400-year-old estate on the Isle of Jersey, an offshore tax haven.

La Hougue was on a list of 72 people and entities about which the Senate Finance Committee is seeking information in connection with its probe of late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell’s longtime associate.

HSBC's stock experienced an upward movement, largely driven by a reassessment of recent geopolitical concerns and positive analyst sentiment. The shares saw a bounce in both London and Hong Kong as investors began to consider that the recent sell-off, linked to China's new cross-border investment rules, may have been overstated. This shift in perception was reinforced by major financial institutions.

JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley both reiterated their "Overweight" ratings on HSBC, suggesting that the impact of the new Chinese Offshore Direct Investment rules on the bank's earnings should be manageable. These reaffirmations from prominent analysts provided a vote of confidence, helping to alleviate investor anxieties that had previously weighed on the stock.

Adding to the positive sentiment, S&P Global Ratings had previously revised its outlook on HSBC Holdings to "positive" from "stable" in late May, affirming its A- long-term issuer credit rating. This upgrade was attributed to HSBC's successful execution of its strategic transformation, its ability to exceed return on tangible equity targets, and robust balance sheet metrics. Furthermore, Erste Group Bank recently increased its earnings per share estimates for HSBC for both fiscal years 2026 and 2027. These positive analyst adjustments and outlook improvements provide a strong fundamental underpinning for the stock's performance.

The bank also recently announced plans to redeem a significant amount of senior unsecured notes due in 2027, an action that signals proactive financial management and could lead to reduced future interest obligations, contributing to a healthier financial outlook. These factors collectively contributed to the stock's positive performance, as the market absorbed more reassuring news regarding its operational stability and future prospects.

sum: The HSBC (LSE: HSBA) share price has soared ahead of other major UK banks, up 26% in the past six months. When comparing performance, it’s clear to see there’s some major differences between the banks.

HSBC may be listed in London and sits in the FTSE 100, but the group generates most of its business in Asia. In 2025, Hong Kong alone contributed about 22% of group revenue, with around $15.9bn of a $71bn total coming from the city.
Meanwhile, profitability remains solid: excluding notable items, return on tangible equity (RoTE) improved to 17% in 2025, up from 16% in 2024.

That Asian tilt helps explain why the shares have outpaced domestic banks. Their performance is increasingly driven by wealth management and corporate banking in Hong Kong, mainland China and Singapore, rather than UK mortgages or current accounts.

Chief executive Georges Elhedery has been very clear on this, saying Asia’s rising middle class and cross‑border wealth flows give the bank “fertile ground for medium‑term growth”, with Hong Kong set to overtake Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross‑border wealth hub by 2030.

So HSBC is moving much more like an Asia‑exposed financial than a pure UK domestic lender. Its share price reacts not just to Bank of England rate decisions, but to Chinese growth data, Hong Kong policy shifts, and capital flows into Asian wealth hubs.
The big question is whether that is a short‑term trend, or the start of a more permanent reframing of HSBC as a gateway to Asian growth.

sum: The FTSE 100 has dropped 0.9% at the open today (5 May), dragged lower by a 5% slump in HSBC (LSE: HSBA) shares after underwhelming results. With oil prices also surging on escalating Middle East tensions, investors may be wondering whether this is a short-term wobble or a sign of deeper pressure on the market.
Q1 earnings from the Asian-focused bank showed a mixed picture, with investors focusing more on rising risks than steady top-line growth.

Revenues rose around 6% year on year, supported by stronger performance in wealth management and higher net interest income. However, sentiment was weighed down by a notable increase in credit losses, which rose to $1.3bn, up $0.4bn from the same period last year.

This was partly driven by a fraud-related charge in UK corporate and institutional banking. In addition, a more cautious economic outlook reflected heightened geopolitical uncertainty and soaring oil prices.

Costs also increased, driven by inflationary pressures, higher performance-related pay, and continued investment in technology. Despite this, management reaffirmed its medium-term targets, including a return on tangible equity of 17% through to 2028.
So are investors reassured by the resilience in revenue or more concerned about the growing signs of credit stress?

The sharp early sell-off reflects a shift in how investors are weighing growth against risk. Revenue growth and profitability remain broadly resilient, but rising credit losses have added to concerns that the economic backdrop is weakening faster than expected.

sum: HSBC Holdings plc HSBC has revived efforts to divest its Australian retail banking business, but the approach has evolved. Instead of selling the entire unit in one transaction, the bank is now prioritizing the sale of its loan portfolio. The news was first reported by The Australian.
First-round non-binding bids are expected by late April, signaling renewed momentum in the process.

HSBC's local operations include a $26-billion loan book alongside $16 billion in deposits, with retail banking, such as mortgages and credit cards, contributing 65% of activity. The divestment strategy resembles HSBC's earlier exit from New Zealand, wherein a phased approach was adopted.
Major players likely to participate include Apollo Global Management, Cerberus Capital Management and Ares Capital Management — all experienced in acquiring loan assets.

This interest mirrors previous transactions in Australia's lending space. Cerberus acquired Westpac's auto loan business in 2021, while Pepper Money, backed by KKR and Pimco, purchased Westpac's $21.4-billion Rams portfolio.

The move reflects HSBC's broader global strategy of concentrating on core markets like Hong Kong and the U.K., while sharpening its presence across Asia. The bank has been actively exiting non-core geographies and reallocating capital toward higher-return regions.

Alongside portfolio restructuring, HSBC is undertaking a sweeping operational overhaul. A partnership with Mistral AI aims to accelerate generative AI adoption, while a $1.5-billion cost-saving program is underway. The bank is also considering workforce reductions as part of a long-term efficiency drive.

Can nothing stop the rampant HSBC share price?
sum: The HSBC (LSE: HSBA) share price is a thing of wonder. It’s up 45% in the last 12 months, and 200% over five years. Normally, when I see past performance like that, I get a little nervous. My worry is that I hop on the bandwagon just as the wheels come off. Is that a risk today?
While HSBC shares look pretty wonderful, that seems to come as standard for FTSE 100 banks these days. They’ve all done well lately.

One reason is that they’ve finally tidied themselves up after the financial crisis. Another is that they’ve been boosted by several years of higher interest rates. These allowed them to widen net interest margins, the difference between what they pay savers and charge borrowers.

HSBC has been making a lot of money as a result. It has a massive opportunity in Asia, notably in China, Hong Kong and Singapore. Plus it recently opened its first Middle East wealth centre in the UAE. This gives it a more diversified earnings base than a purely UK-focused bank.

In 2024, it posted bumper pre-tax profits of $32.3bn, up 6.6% from $30.3bn the year before. Profits dipped in 2025 to $29.9bn, but that was largely due to one-offs impairments, legal provisions and restructuring costs. Even so, it’s still a huge number, and the board handsomely rewarded shareholders, hiking the full-year dividend by 13.6%. In the five years since the pandemic, HSBC has increased shareholder payouts at an average compound rate of around 38% a year. Few FTSE 100 companies can match that.

HSBC has also been incredibly generous with share buybacks, which totalled $6bn last year. These have now been put on hold for nine months as it spends £13.6bn completing its stake in Hang Seng Bank. Investors will be hoping they resume after that.

Management has been simplifying the group, exiting weaker markets and focusing on core strengths such as wealth management. It’s now targeting an improved tangible return on equity of 17%, combined with a dividend payout ratio of around 50% of earnings. Today, the trailing yield is 4.4%. That’s forecast to hit 4.48% this year and 5.28% in 2027.

Bank Warns of Tesla Stock Collapse
sum: In its quest to pivot from selling EVs to AI and humanoid robots, Tesla has seen his core business get eviscerated.

The company hit a four-year sales low in the United States earlier this year, with no signs of imminent recovery. That’s coming to bear on its share price, which is already down almost 20 percent year to date, signaling that even its notoriously die-hard investors — who have propped up its lofty valuation of well over $1 trillion while its financials have tanked — are starting to get antsy.

Banks are equally unimpressed, with analysts warning that the situation is set to get even worse. Case in point, HSBC stock analyst Mike Tyndall recently reiterated a “reduce” rating on Tesla, which he originally set at the start of the year. As The Street reports, he’s expecting the company’s shares to fall from today’s price of around $365 to just $131 over the next year, an enormous wipeout of over 60 percent — and that’s without getting into the its starry high of $480 or so just last year.

Tyndall argued that Tesla will see immense pressure in the EV industry, especially as the competition continues to grow and markets become more regionalized outside of the US, particularly in Europe and China. He also argued that the company was overestimating global growth opportunities.

Beyond waning EV sales, Tesla is struggling to ramp up production of its two-seater Cybercab, a key component of CEO Elon Musk’s efforts to establish a robotaxi service. The company is looking to start mass production of the vehicle next month, officials told the Wall Street Journal, in a major test of its efforts to pivot away from being a traditional car business.

Tesla is also struggling to get its controversial and misleadingly-named Full Self-Driving advanced driver assistance feature okayed abroad. A key litmus test for the feature is playing out in the Netherlands, where its approval is currently pending. If authorized, the rest of the European Union could follow later this summer, if the company is to be believed.

But that’s far from a guarantee, as Electrek points out. If regulators deny the company’s application, it could signal even more tough days ahead for Musk’s flagship autonomous driving ambitions outside of the US.

HSBC says stock markets are pricing in a recession, not stagflation. Here's how it’s trading the rotation
sum: - The likelihood of looming stagflation 'has barely moved," according to HSBC strategists - but equity markets appear to be pricing in a recession
- They named countries and sectors where there could be buying opportunities for investors.
- Emerging markets and cyclical stocks were highlighted in the Tuesday note.

Equity markets appear to be pricing in a recession as the U.S.-Iran war drags on — but heavy selling pressure has opened up some buying opportunities for investors, according to HSBC strategists. In a note published by the banking giant on Tuesday, Alastair Pinder and Pankaj Agarwala said volatility in the oil market had caused "dislocations in equity markets." Since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran at the end of February, surging oil prices have sparked fears of a 1970s-style stagflation. But HSBC's team said they believe recent equity rotations tell a different story. "Talk of a shift toward stagflation is building, but we would argue equity markets price action is more indicative of trading for a recessionary outcome," they said. "Our regime models show the equity market is now pricing a 35% probability of recession, up from 10% just two weeks ago, while the implied likelihood of stagflation has barely moved, holding at 8%." Emerging markets, industrials and banks Pinder and Agarwala outlined where they see opportunities for investors in the current environment. They said global equities had fallen by around 5% since the start of the Iran war — but noted their machine learning systems suggested the overall move was largely justified. "Still, underneath the surface there appears to be a number of dislocations," they said. "We believe Korea, South Africa and Indonesia have been oversold by about 5-10%, leaving valuations that look increasingly attractive, especially as our work shows these markets are not among the most exposed to higher oil prices." South Korea's Kospi index was the world's top-performing stock market in 2025, but has seen historic volatility since the war broke out, thanks to its concentration of memory giants and its sensitivity to energy prices.

sum: HSBC stock traded at EUR 15.09 on Lang & Schwarz at 18:18 CET on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. That was 1.63 percent below the EUR 15.34 quote in the latest relevant report at 12:12 CET the same day, giving investors a fresh capital-market update without establishing a causal link to the bank's operating performance.

HSBC reported its third-quarter results on October 27. In the HSBC 3Q 2026 earnings release, profit before tax rose 32 percent year on year to USD 9.6 billion, while profit after tax increased 38 percent to USD 7.6 billion.

The headline profit comparison includes a USD 1.4 billion benefit from the non-recurrence of legal provisions recorded in the year-earlier quarter. Excluding notable items and on a constant-currency basis, profit before tax increased to USD 10.0 billion. Revenue reached USD 18.6 billion, net interest income rose 6 percent to USD 9.3 billion and expected credit losses declined 17 percent to USD 0.8 billion.

HSBC also retained its medium-term targets. The bank continues to expect banking net interest income of at least USD 46 billion in 2026 and targets return on tangible equity of at least 17 percent for 2026 through 2028, excluding notable items. Its 50 percent dividend payout target also remains unchanged.

The board approved a third interim dividend of USD 0.10 per share. HSBC completed its previous USD 1 billion buyback on September 28 and intends to launch another programme of up to USD 1 billion before announcing its 2026 full-year results. The planned distribution adds a direct shareholder-return element while investors continue to assess the durability of underlying income growth and cost discipline.

items.t: Antique begins Buy call on Canara HSBC Life shares
sum: Antique Stock Broking has initiated coverage of Canara HSBC Life Insurance Co. Ltd., assigning a “Buy” recommendation and outlining its view on the insurer’s risk-return profile as the company lifts its protection business and maintains bancassurance-led growth in India. The initiation follows Canara HSBC Life’s first year as a listed company on the BSE and NSE. Antique has set a target price of ₹190 per share, indicating potential upside of about 26.7% from the previous close. The brokerage’s estimates place the stock at 1.7 times and 1.5 times its projected price-to-embedded value for fiscal years 2027 and 2028, respectively.

In its initiation report cited by Business Standard, Antique said Canara HSBC Life recorded an individual weighted premium income (WPI) compound annual growth rate of about 21% over fiscal 2015-25, with growth of roughly 20% in year-to-date fiscal 2026. Over the same period, Indian life insurance industry growth on this metric was around 10% to 11%, according to the brokerage. The company’s individual WPI market share increased from 1.6% in fiscal 2015 to 2.9% in year-to-date fiscal 2026. Recently disclosed results for the nine months ended Dec. 31, 2025, are consistent with that trend. Individual WPI reached ₹1,915.3 crore, up 20.5% year on year. Total annualized premium equivalent (APE) was ₹2,095 crore, a 22.3% rise from ₹1,713.3 crore a year earlier.

New business premium from individual and group lines grew 28.1% year on year to ₹2,929.4 crore, and renewal premium rose 34.4% to ₹4,001.9 crore. Total premium income for the period was ₹6,931.4 crore, an increase of 31.6%. Assets under management stood at ₹46,888.7 crore, up 17.2% from the prior-year period. Profit after tax was ₹91.9 crore for the nine months, 8.2% higher than a year earlier. On an APE basis, the product mix comprised unit-linked products at 61%, annuities at 12%, non-participating savings at 13%, non-participating protection at 7%, and participating products at 5%. Persistency ratios were reported at 85.6% for the 13th month and 59.2% for the 61st month.

items.t: Barclays and HSBC shares are plunging today – is this my moment?
sum: I’ve been looking for an opportunity to buy HSBC (LSE: HSBA) shares and I really fancy Barclays (LSE: BARC) too. Is this my chance?
I already hold Lloyds Banking Group, which I bought three years ago, and it’s been a superb investment. To be fair, all the big banks have.

The sector has been on a tear as higher inflation and interest rates widen net interest margins, the gap between what banks pay savers and charge borrowers. I’ve got spare cash in my SIPP and have been considering splitting it between Barclays and HSBC. I think they’d nicely balance my holding in Lloyds.
Lloyds is now largely a low-key domestic lender focused on UK households and small businesses. Barclays and HSBC are much bigger beasts.

Barclays still runs a sizeable corporate and investment bank in the US, while HSBC has huge exposure to Asia via Hong Kong and China. Both are targeting the Middle East too. That brings opportunity, but also risk, as today’s market moves show.

Barclays is one of the biggest faller’s on the FTSE 100 as Iran spooks markets, down more than 5% this morning. HSBC has dropped almost 4%. Banks are on the front line when geopolitical nerves are frazzled, particularly these two. UK-focused NatWest Group is down 3.3%, and Lloyds 2.8%.

One thing has stopped me from buying bank shares recently: they’ve just done too well. Barclays is up 50% over one year and 180% over five, while. HSBC has climbed 53% and 225% respectively. I’m wary of rocking up just as the party ends. Now I’m wondering if today’s dip is the invitation I’ve been waiting for.

sum: Europe's largest lender HSBC on Wednesday reported annual pre-tax profit of $29.91 billion, beating analysts' estimates on the back of a strong performance in its wealth division and Hong Kong businesses.
While annual profit declined 7.4%, HSBC's revenue gained 4%, year on year, and both exceeded estimates.
Here are HSBC's full-year results compared with the consensus estimates compiled by the bank.

The lender's fourth-quarter profit before tax rose to $6.8 billion, up $4.5 billion from a year earlier, largely due to favorable one-off items linked to business disposals. Operating expenses rose 8% to $9.3 billion, reflecting restructuring costs, technology investment and higher performance-related pay.
Its revenue for the final quarter jumped 42% year on year to $16.4 billion.

HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery said in a statement that 2025 marked a year of "decisive action and swift execution," with all four of the bank's businesses performing well and building strong momentum.
The lender now aims to deliver a return on average tangible equity — a measure of profitability — of 17% or more, excluding notable items, in between 2026 and 2028. RoTE was 13.3% in 2025.

A quiet investing revolution is underway in Europe
sum: Across the continent, the market for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) has been growing rapidly, as individual (or “retail”) investors use monthly plans to channel their hard-earned savings into funds containing index-based products.

According to a study commissioned by BlackRock’s iShares platform, 10.8 million ETF savings plans worth EUR 17.6 billion were executed in 2024, significantly higher than the 7.6m plans involving EUR 15 billion that were in place at the end of the previous year. The trend has been especially pronounced in Germany, where government policy allowing easier access to the capital markets for retirement savings has helped.

The study noted “an increasing number of private investors [in Europe] turning to index-based products as a means of building up their assets”. By the end of August 2024, about two trillion euros had been invested in ETFs in Europe – an impressive 40 per cent increase in volume compared to the end of 2023.

This reflects what we believe is an ongoing, generational shift in investor preferences for the convenience and cost-effectiveness of ETFs, as a way to gain exposure to investment narratives that are defining our age. These run from shifting consumer tastes and sustainability to industrial and technology themes such as AI. Recently, cybersecurity and defence have been added to the mix.

Yet in the UK, the picture is still evolving. While there is huge pent-up demand for savings products, ETF adoption by retail investors remains stuck in the slow lane. We estimate that ETF use is around eight per cent of all UK investors, compared with the US at almost 60 per cent. Yet, there is an estimated £610bn tucked away in cash (based on the FCA’s Financial Lives survey conducted in May 2024) that British savers might channel into investments such as ETFs, if some pipes were unblocked.
One of the barriers to widespread adoption in the UK has been the suboptimal way in which ETFs are purchased.

Let’s say an investor wants to buy £50 worth of ETFs each month via a wealth platform, but because ETFs are traded on stock exchanges in single units (like company shares), this fixed monthly amount will rarely result in the purchase of a round number of units.
